title: Zero-Knowledge
tagline: Prove you know a secret, or that you are old enough, without revealing the secret or your age. What makes such a proof convincing, and what quietly breaks it?

client.name: Prover
client.brief: Knows a secret or holds a credential. Wants to convince without revealing.

application.name: Verifier
application.brief: Wants to be convinced, and should learn nothing beyond the one fact.

idp.name: Issuer
idp.brief: Signs the credentials proofs rest on, and runs any setup they need.

mcp.name: Service
mcp.brief: Acts on the verifier's verdict: opens the door, sells the ticket.

teaches: A zero-knowledge proof convinces the verifier of one statement and reveals nothing else.
Order is everything: the prover commits first, and only then meets a challenge she could not predict.
A proof has to be tied to this verifier and this moment, or it can be copied and replayed.
A proof can be perfectly valid and still be about the wrong statement, or rest on the wrong issuer.

glossary.means: A value the prover fixes before the challenge. It locks her in without revealing her secret.
An unpredictable value from the verifier that the prover must answer.
Someone who doesn't know the secret almost never passes.
Proving one fact from a credential (over 18) without showing the rest (name, birth date).
A value used once, so that an old proof can't be reused.
A one-time ceremony some proof systems need. Its leftover randomness must be destroyed, or proofs can be forged.
